reason: The provided sources contain rich, cross-verified details covering the mission's dramatic history, unique orbital trajectory around Jupiter, and key scientific discoveries.
story: To explore the Sun's uncharted polar regions, scientists needed a spacecraft to leave the ecliptic plane of the Solar System—a maneuver impossible for standard rockets. The joint ESA-NASA mission Ulysses was designed to fly out to Jupiter first, using the giant planet's gravitational pull to slingshot into a high-inclination solar orbit. Originally planned as a two-probe mission, budget cuts reduced it to one, and the 1986 Challenger disaster delayed its launch until October 1990. Launched from Space Shuttle Discovery with a specialized nuclear RTG power source, Ulysses became the fastest human-made object accelerated from Earth at that time. During its 18-year mission—over four times its expected lifetime—Ulysses made nearly three full solar orbits, unexpectedly flew through three comet tails, and revealed that the Sun's polar magnetic fields are unexpectedly weak while interstellar dust entering the Solar System is 30 times more abundant than previously believed.
angle: To look down at the Sun's unexplored poles, a spacecraft had to fly all the way out to Jupiter first just to slingshot itself out of the Solar System's plane.

claims.claim: Ulysses was a joint deep-space mission conducted by the European Space Agency (ESA) and NASA.
The probe launched in October 1990 aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on mission STS-41.
The mission was originally conceived as a two-spacecraft project before NASA canceled its spacecraft in 1981.
The launch of Ulysses was significantly delayed following the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger disaster.
Ulysses was boosted toward Jupiter using an Inertial Upper Stage (IUS) and a Payload Assist Module (PAM-S).
To reach a high-inclination orbit over the Sun's poles, Ulysses performed a gravity assist flyby around Jupiter in February 1992.
Because solar panels could not generate enough power at Jupiter's distance, Ulysses was powered by a Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG).
Upon leaving Earth, Ulysses became the fastest human-made object ever accelerated from Earth up to that point.
Ulysses became the first space probe to survey the space environment above and below the poles of the Sun.
Data from Ulysses revealed that the magnetic field emanating from the Sun's poles is much weaker than previously assumed.
Ulysses measured interstellar dust coming into the Solar System and discovered it was 30 times more abundant than previously expected.
Ulysses showed that the solar wind had grown progressively weaker over time, reaching a 50-year low by 2008.
During its voyage, Ulysses unexpectedly flew through the ion tails of three comets, including Comet Hyakutake in May 1996.
Ulysses operated for over 18 years—more than four times its planned design life—before ground controllers shut down communications on June 30, 2009.
As power from the RTG depleted, mission operators faced the risk of hydrazine fuel freezing inside the spacecraft's attitude control lines.
The main spacecraft structure for Ulysses was built by German aerospace manufacturer Dornier Systems.
